claim: Anthropic says to use API on-demand compaction wherever available, choose threshold compaction when you want the API to manage context inside ordinary requests, and use your own summarizer when you already run one that replaces the whole history.
why: On-demand compaction lets you control when it happens, run it in the background and keep recent turns word for word, while threshold compaction runs inside the request that reaches the trigger and cannot run in the background.
check: For an API agent that compacts, look at which of the three routes it uses; a hand-rolled summarizer or a blocking threshold setup with no reason to avoid on-demand compaction is a finding.
quote: Use on-demand compaction wherever it is available.

claim: On-demand API compaction can leave recent turns verbatim and summarize only older turns, and a custom summarization prompt can replace the default one when the summary drops something a later turn needs.
why: Keeping recent turns preserves their exact wording, while a custom prompt can tell the summarizer which details to carry forward.
check: If an agent loses detail after on-demand compaction, check whether it needs recent turns kept verbatim or a custom summary prompt for details that must survive summarization.
quote: when the default summary drops something a later turn needs. Your prompt replaces the default one.

claim: Anthropic calls server-side compaction the primary strategy for long conversations in most use cases and recommends context editing for scenarios that need finer control over what is cleared.
why: Server-side compaction requires no client-side summarization code, while context editing lets an application selectively clear old tool results or thinking blocks.
check: An API setup that hand-builds clearing or summarization logic for an ordinary long conversation, with no need for fine-grained control, is a candidate to simplify to server-side compaction.
quote: is the primary strategy for managing context in long-running conversations. The strategies on this page are useful for specific scenarios where you need more fine-grained control over what content is cleared.

claim: Tool result clearing (clear_tool_uses_20250919) defaults to triggering above 100,000 input tokens and keeping the 3 most recent tool use/result pairs, clearing only results unless clear_tool_inputs is set to true, and has no clear_at_least or exclude_tools unless you set them.
why: The defaults decide when and how much is cleared, and exclude_tools lets a setup exempt tools whose calls and results should never be cleared.
check: Check a context_management config for whether the defaults fit the workload, and whether tools whose results must persist (such as a plan or memory tool) are listed in exclude_tools.
quote: 100,000 input tokens | Defines when the context editing strategy activates. Once the prompt exceeds this threshold, clearing starts.

claim: Clearing tool results invalidates the cached prompt prefix every time it fires, so a clearing config should set clear_at_least to a size that makes the cache rewrite worthwhile.
why: Each clearing event costs a cache write, and clearing a few tokens at a time pays that cost repeatedly for little saving.
check: If a context_management edit has trigger set low and no clear_at_least, flag that it can bust the cache for small gains.
quote: Tool result clearing:** Invalidates cached prompt prefixes when content is cleared. To account for this, clear enough tokens to make the cache invalidation worthwhile.

claim: Adding the clear_thinking_20251015 strategy without a keep value applies keep of one thinking turn on every model, including models whose default keeps all prior thinking, so adding the strategy can reduce thinking retention and invalidate the cache.
why: The per-model default of keeping all thinking applies only when the strategy is absent, which makes an unconfigured strategy an override rather than a no-op.
check: Check requests that omit keep for unintended reductions in thinking retention on models that keep all thinking by default, and check that code shared across model classes sets keep explicitly.
quote: A request that includes this strategy without `keep` gets `{type: "thinking_turns", value: 1}` on every model, including models whose [per-model default](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#thinking-block-clearing) keeps all thinking.

claim: On the models with preserved thinking, server-side context management never invalidates thinking blocks, whereas client-side edits to earlier turns can invalidate the thinking blocks of every later assistant turn.
why: On these models, editing earlier turns on the client can cause later thinking blocks to fail the preserved-thinking prefix check.
check: For an agent on one of these models that trims or rewrites old messages in its own code, check whether it should use server-side context editing or compaction instead.
quote: server-side context management never invalidates thinking blocks. Client-side edits to earlier turns can invalidate the thinking blocks in every later assistant turn.

claim: When thinking block clearing and tool result clearing are combined in one context_management request, the clear_thinking_20251015 strategy must come first in the edits array.
why: The API requires that order when several strategies are used.
check: Check the order of the edits array in any request that combines both strategies.
quote: When using multiple strategies, you must list the `clear_thinking_20251015` strategy first in the `edits` array.

claim: When context editing is combined with the memory tool, Claude receives an automatic warning as the conversation approaches the clearing threshold so it can save important tool results to memory files before they are cleared.
why: The warning gives Claude a chance to save essential information to memory before the tool results are removed from its active context.
check: If important results need to survive clearing, check whether Claude can use the memory tool to save them before they are cleared.
quote: Claude receives an automatic warning to preserve important information. This allows Claude to save tool results or context to its memory files before they’re cleared from the conversation history.

claim: The built-in client-side SDK compaction prompt has five parts covering the task and success criteria, current state and artifacts, discoveries and failed approaches, next steps and blockers, and context to preserve such as preferences and commitments.
why: The structure is meant to let work resume without losing context or repeating mistakes.
check: For a custom SDK compaction prompt used to resume work, check whether it carries forward the decisions, failed approaches, and commitments the resumed task depends on.
quote:
1. **Task Overview:** The user’s core request, success criteria, and constraints.
2. **Current State:** What has been completed, files modified, and artifacts produced.
3. **Important Discoveries:** Technical constraints, decisions made, errors resolved, and failed approaches.
4. **Next Steps:** Specific actions needed, blockers, and priority order.

claim: The default client-side SDK compaction prompt tells Claude to err on the side of including information that prevents duplicate work or repeated mistakes, including failed approaches and why they failed, decisions and their rationale, and promises to the user.
why: Recording these details helps the next context window resume the task without repeating failed work or losing track of commitments.
check: If a custom SDK compaction prompt asks only for progress, check whether unresolved commitments or failed approaches needed on resumption would survive.
quote: Be concise but complete—err on the side of including information that would prevent duplicate work or repeated mistakes. Write in a way that enables immediate resumption of the task.

claim: Anthropic lists precise recall of early conversation details, exact state across many variables, and extensive server-side tool use as less suitable for client-side SDK compaction, and calls tasks that produce persistent artifacts good fits.
why: Client-side SDK compaction replaces the full history with a summary, while artifacts outside the conversation remain available.
check: For a workflow whose correctness depends on early exact details, check that those details are written to a file or memory and not left to the summary.
quote:
Tasks that produce artifacts (files, reports) that persist outside the conversation

**Less ideal use cases:**

* Tasks requiring precise recall of early conversation details
* Workflows using server-side tools extensively
* Tasks that need to maintain exact state across many variables

claim: Client-side SDK compaction (compaction_control in the TypeScript and Ruby tool runners) is deprecated and was removed from the Python SDK in v1.0, and Anthropic recommends server-side compaction via the compact_20260112 edit in context_management.
why: Server-side compaction has less integration complexity and better token calculation; SDK compaction can also trigger prematurely after server-side tools because cache reads from internal calls inflate its token total.
check: Check whether continued use of compaction_control serves a specific need for client-side summarization control, and use server-side compaction when a Python SDK v1.0 or later tool runner needs compaction.
quote: The `compaction_control` parameter is deprecated in the TypeScript and Ruby SDKs and will be removed in a future version. The TypeScript and Ruby SDKs emit a deprecation warning when it is enabled. The Python SDK removed it in v1.0.

claim: The memory tool is client-side: Claude only requests file operations under /memories and the application's own handler executes them against storage it controls, so persistence, size caps and expiry are the application's job.
why: The memory store lives in the application, so its handler is responsible for safeguards such as path validation and size limits.
check: Look at the memory tool handler for path validation, per-file size caps and cleanup of long-unused files.
quote: The memory tool operates client-side: Claude requests file operations, and your application runs them. You control where and how the data is stored through your own infrastructure.

claim: When the memory tool is in a request's tools, the API automatically adds a memory protocol to the system prompt telling Claude to view its memory directory first and to assume interruption, and the tool description already tells Claude to keep the directory organized.
why: The API supplies the memory protocol and tool description, and Anthropic says a prompt can reinforce organization if Claude still creates cluttered files.
check: Check for redundant copies of the built-in memory protocol when the memory tool is enabled, and consider whether any added organization guidance addresses observed clutter.
quote: the API automatically adds this instruction to the system prompt. You don’t need to send it yourself:

claim: Anthropic suggests considering the memory tool alongside compaction for long-running agents, so compaction keeps the active context small and memory preserves information that must survive summarization.
why: Compaction summarizes conversation history, while Claude can retrieve durable notes from memory files on demand.
check: For a long-running agent that relies on compaction alone, check whether durable facts, progress and decisions are also written to memory or files.
quote: compaction keeps the active context small without client-side bookkeeping, and memory preserves the information that must survive summarization.

claim: A memory tool handler must validate every path in every command, because a path such as /memories/../../secrets.env can reach files outside the memory directory; Anthropic lists canonical-path resolution, rejecting ../ and URL-encoded traversal as safeguards.
why: The application executes the file operations, so it must prevent requests from accessing files outside the memory directory.
check: Check that every memory command validates its paths against the memory root, for example by resolving each path to its canonical form and checking that it remains inside the directory.
quote: Your implementation must validate every path in every command to prevent directory traversal attacks.

claim: Anthropic removed over 80 percent of Claude Code's system prompt for models like Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5 with no measurable loss on its coding evaluations.
why: Anthropic found that it could remove many constraints that had been needed to avoid worst cases and let newer models use surrounding context and judgment.
check: When migrating a Claude Code prompt to these models, review old guardrails and use coding evaluations to check whether removing them changes results.
quote: We removed over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt for models like Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5 with no measurable loss on our coding evaluations.

claim: Overlapping or conflicting instructions across the system prompt, skills, CLAUDE.md and the user request, such as 'leave documentation as appropriate' next to 'DO NOT add comments', make Claude think harder about which to follow before it acts.
why: Anthropic saw such clashes in its own Claude Code transcripts and concluded it had been overconstraining the model.
check: Compare the system prompt, CLAUDE.md, skills, and the request for overlapping or conflicting guidance that makes Claude decide which instruction to follow.
quote: Generally, Claude can interpret the user’s intent to get to the right answer, but Claude must think more carefully about these overlapping and conflicting messages before deciding what to do.

claim: For the newest models Anthropic replaced absolute rules, such as 'default to writing no comments', with a judgment cue ('write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom').
why: Strong guidance written to prevent worst cases on older models is wrong for some prompts, and newer models handle those decisions without explicit rules.
check: Flag always/never style rules in instruction files that a judgment-based line could replace, especially those about style or documentation.
quote: But newer models have better judgement and can handle these decisions well without explicit rules.

claim: For its newest models Anthropic found that giving tool-use examples constrains them to a certain exploration space, and advises designing expressive tool parameters (for example an enum of statuses plus a one-line behavior rule) instead of adding examples.
why: An expressive parameter such as a status enum can hint at how to use the tool, while examples can anchor the model to demonstrated behavior, qualifying the older example-count guidance in prompting-070 for this use case.
check: Check tool descriptions and skills for example blocks that dictate one way to call a tool, and whether a parameter enum or schema would convey the same thing.
quote: With our newest models, we’ve found that giving examples actually constrains them to a certain exploration space.

claim: Anthropic calls it a myth that CLAUDE.md and SKILL.md should be a central repository of every practice and advises a tree of files loaded at the right time, such as moving verification and code review into skills the model calls selectively, and referencing them from CLAUDE.md.
why: Progressive disclosure loads guidance when needed, while CLAUDE.md imports load with their parent (context-013).
check: Look for a CLAUDE.md that embeds long review, verification or release procedures, and check whether they could be skills referenced by one line.
quote: A common myth is that you want to make these a central repository for every known practice that you might run into, because Claude would not find it otherwise. Instead, consider having a tree of files that can be loaded at the right time.

claim: Anthropic found it could remove repeated examples from the Claude Code system prompt and put tool-use instructions in the tool descriptions, while earlier models sometimes needed repetition or favored instructions near the end of the context window.
why: The tool description can carry the usage instructions that Anthropic previously repeated in the system prompt, while prompting-060 still protects working redundancy.
check: Check for redundant tool-use instructions in the system prompt that can live in the tool description alone.
quote: We found we could delete these repeat examples and put instructions on how to use tools in the tool descriptions rather than the system prompt.

claim: Anthropic says the # hotkey habit of writing notes into CLAUDE.md is superseded because Claude now saves relevant memories automatically, and that Claude used to rely on CLAUDE.md as its memory but now also has memory, artifacts and skills for carrying context across sessions.
why: Claude Code can now carry context across sessions using memory, artifacts, and skills, so session notes need not all live in CLAUDE.md.
check: Check whether the setup still encourages users to save notes to CLAUDE.md with the # hotkey, a practice Anthropic used to encourage before Claude saved relevant memories automatically.
quote: We used to encourage users to save things to Claude’s memory, by using the # hotkey to write to their CLAUDE.md automatically. Instead, Claude now automatically saves memories that are relevant to the work and to you.

claim: Anthropic recommends keeping CLAUDE.md short, briefly describing the repo, and spending most of the tokens on codebase gotchas.
why: A repo-specific convention such as keeping all types in one file is the kind of gotcha Anthropic suggests documenting.
check: Check whether CLAUDE.md covers codebase gotchas and skips details about the layout, language, or framework that Claude can already see in the repo.
quote: Keep your CLAUDE.md lightweight and briefly describe what your repo is for, but spend most of the tokens on gotchas inside of the codebase.

claim: Anthropic advises treating skills as lightweight guides that Claude uses to find information when needed, avoiding overconstraint except in highly important areas, splitting long skills into many files, and encoding opinions, knowledge or practices particular to the user, team or product.
why: Generic best practices the model already knows add tokens, while team-specific knowledge is what the model cannot supply.
check: For long skills, check whether supporting detail could be loaded from separate files when needed and whether the main instructions capture practices specific to the user, team, or product.
quote: It’s best when skills encode particular opinions, knowledge, or best practices that are particular to you, your team, or product.

claim: Anthropic recommends giving Claude references in code form, such as a detailed test suite, a function to port or an HTML mockup, rather than prose or screenshots, and using rubrics that verifier agents can apply to taste-based quality.
why: Code is high-fidelity instruction in a language Claude knows very well, and an HTML mockup generally beats a description or a screenshot.
check: For tasks with a design or behavior spec, check whether the spec is given as a test, an executable reference or a mockup instead of a prose description alone.
quote: Generally you should prefer files that are in code as it provides clear, high-fidelity instructions to Claude in a language it knows very well.

claim: In its earlier harness work, Anthropic observed premature wrap-up near the context limit on Claude Sonnet 4.5, added context resets to address it, and found the behavior absent when it ran the same harness on Claude Opus 4.5.
why: Harnesses encode assumptions about what the model cannot do, and those assumptions go stale as models improve.
check: If a harness still resets context to prevent Sonnet 4.5-style premature wrap-up, retest whether that reset helps on the model actually in use.
quote: As just one example, in prior work we found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 would wrap up tasks prematurely as it sensed its context limit approaching—a behavior sometimes called “context anxiety.” We addressed this by adding context resets to the harness. But when we used the same harness on Claude Opus 4.5, we found that the behavior was gone. The resets had become dead weight.

claim: Anthropic warns that a harness can recover messages removed by compaction only if it stores the original messages.
why: When compaction, memory writes, or trimming decide what to keep, it is hard to predict which tokens future turns will need.
check: If a custom harness must recover earlier messages after compaction, check that it stores and can retrieve the originals.
quote: If messages are transformed by a compaction step, the harness removes compacted messages from Claude’s context window, and these are recoverable only if they are stored.

claim: Managed Agents keeps credentials out of reach of Claude-generated code running in the sandbox.
why: Narrow token scopes still rely on assumptions about what Claude can do with a limited token.
check: Check whether code can read Git or MCP credentials from inside the sandbox, using Managed Agents' Git remotes wired at sandbox setup and vault-backed MCP proxy as examples of how to keep credentials out of the code's reach.
quote: The structural fix was to make sure the tokens are never reachable from the sandbox where Claude’s generated code runs.

claim: Claude Managed Agents is a hosted, pre-built agent harness (loop, sandbox, tool execution, prompt caching and compaction) that Anthropic positions for long-running and asynchronous work, whereas the Messages API is for custom agent loops and fine-grained control.
why: Managed Agents removes the need to build the agent loop and runtime, at the price of a managed, stateful service in beta (header managed-agents-2026-04-01).
check: When a team has built its own agent loop, sandbox and compaction purely for long-running background work, note that Anthropic offers Managed Agents for that case; when it needs custom loops, the Messages API is the documented fit.
quote: Instead of building your own agent loop, tool execution, and runtime, you get a fully managed environment where Claude can read files, run commands, browse the web, and run code securely. The harness supports built-in prompt caching, compaction, and other performance optimizations for high-quality, efficient agent outputs.

claim: Claude Managed Agents is ineligible for HIPAA BAA coverage and for Zero Data Retention, with a Zero Data Retention exception for self-hosted Managed Agents.
why: Hosted Managed Agents is stateful and stores conversation history, sandbox state, and outputs server-side, whereas self-hosted users store that data themselves.
check: If an integration requires Zero Data Retention or HIPAA BAA coverage, check whether it uses hosted Managed Agents, which the overview excludes from both.
quote: Not eligible for ZDR, except for self-hosted Managed Agents. Sessions are stateful resources; transcripts persist until you delete them.

claim: Anthropic recommends Managed Agents multiagent coordination for complex work that spans different areas or breaks into well-scoped tasks serving one goal.
why: Each agent runs in an isolated context, which can improve output quality and time to completion, and each agent in a run uses tokens.
check: Check whether the work has independent subtasks to run in parallel, parts that need specialists with focused prompts and tools, or complex subtasks to escalate to a more capable model.
quote: Multiagent coordination is best suited for complex tasks that either require work across a variety of surfaces or consist of multiple well-scoped tasks that contribute to an overall goal.

claim: Anthropic recommends dynamic workflows for most Managed Agents work that needs multiple agents.
why: Workflow runs orchestrate agents programmatically in the background, freeing the main agent to interact with the user.
check: Check whether the setup uses dynamic workflows for work with many pieces, parallel tasks, or long tasks that should finish sooner.
quote: Most work that needs more than one agent: work with many pieces, parallel work, or a long task that should complete sooner. Examples are audits, migrations, deep research, and cross-checking.

claim: Managed Agents subagent delegation is one level deep and a session can have at most 25 child threads at a time, idle ones included, while advisor threads and a workflow run's threads do not count toward the 25.
why: Idle subagent threads stay available until archived, so they keep counting against the limit.
check: For a lead agent that spawns many subagents over a long session, check that finished subagent threads are archived so the 25-thread limit is not hit.
quote: Delegation is one level deep, and a session can have at most 25 child threads at a time, idle ones included.

claim: With the multiagent_20261001 type, subagents and workflows are both enabled by default and inline agents are on under each, so an agent configured only for an advisor can still delegate and start workflow runs unless both are set to disabled.
why: Omitting subagents and workflows from a new block uses their enabled defaults, and setting either of those two settings to null turns it back on.
check: Look at the multiagent block of an agent that is meant to work alone or only consult an advisor and check that subagents and workflows are explicitly disabled.
quote: By default, `subagents` and `workflows` are both enabled.

claim: Managed Agents pins referenced predefined_agents to the resolved versions when the parent agent is created or an update sends the list, and an update that omits the list retains the existing pins.
why: The parent's configuration is snapshotted at save time.
check: If the lead should use a newer reviewer or specialist, check that its updated predefined_agents list resolves to the intended version.
quote: Referenced agents stay pinned to the versions resolved then and don’t pick up later updates to their definitions. An update that doesn’t send the list keeps the versions that are already pinned.

claim: A Managed Agents inline agent has no saved agent definition and uses the session agent's model, tools, and MCP servers, so a helper needs a predefined agent in the relevant list to use a different model or a narrower tool set than the session agent.
why: A predefined agent uses its own configuration, while an inline agent inherits the session agent's model and tool set.
check: For a workflow that fans out many agents on the session's top model, check whether routine stages could use listed cheaper predefined agents.
quote: An agent that is not saved. The agent that the session runs, or a workflow, defines it when it hands out the work. It uses that agent’s model, tools, MCP servers, and skills.

claim: In Managed Agents, MCP servers are declared per agent but vault credentials apply to every session thread, and to limit helpers to different MCP servers you can use predefined agents that declare only the servers they need because inline agents inherit the session agent's servers.
why: An inline agent has no definition and inherits the session agent's MCP servers, and every vault credential in the session is available to every thread.
check: Check that vault_ids covers the MCP servers used across the session, that predefined agents declare only the servers they need, and that inline_agents is disabled where only listed agents should run.
quote: To limit an agent’s access, declare only the servers it needs in its agent definition. You can’t limit an inline agent this way.

claim: Managed Agents subagents all share one sandbox and filesystem while each has its own context-isolated thread, so parallel agents writing the same files can collide even though their conversations are separate.
why: Only conversation history is isolated, not the filesystem or the vault credentials.
check: For parallel agents, check that each writes to distinct paths or that results are returned and merged by one agent.
quote: All agents share the same sandbox, filesystem, and [vault credentials](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/vaults), but each agent runs in its own **session thread**, a context-isolated event stream with its own conversation history.

claim: For Managed Agents dynamic workflows, Anthropic advises telling the agent in its system prompt which tasks call for a workflow run and which small tasks it should do itself (its example: start a run for more than a few contracts, review one or two directly), and keeping runs to tasks that need them.
why: The agent decides on its own when to start a run and every agent in a run uses tokens.
check: Check that a system prompt for an agent with workflows enabled names the size or kind of task that warrants a run and the cases to handle solo.
quote: To adapt it, name the tasks in your agent’s domain that call for a run, and the small tasks the agent should do itself.

claim: Managed Agents lets a system prompt ask the agent to describe a workflow run and wait for approval, but the harness has no approval step that enforces the instruction before the run starts.
why: The agent starts runs on its own judgment and permission policies cover only the tools a run's agents call, not the start of the run.
check: Check that a Managed Agents setup requiring a spending cap uses a session budget instead of relying on an instruction to wait for approval.
quote: There’s no approval step before a run starts, so nothing enforces this.

claim: To cap spending across a Managed Agents session and its workflow runs, set the session budget at creation because it cannot be added later, and runs pause when the session reaches it.
why: Every agent in a run uses tokens, and that usage counts toward the session budget.
check: For a Managed Agents session that needs a spending cap covering its workflow runs, check that the session budget is set at creation.
quote: to cap the session’s spend, runs included; you can’t add one to an existing session. Runs pause when the session reaches the budget

claim: In Managed Agents the advisor model must meet a minimum capability level and the agent's own model must not be more capable than its advisor, though equal-capability models can pair, and an invalid pairing is rejected with a 400 when the agent is saved and again at session creation.
why: The advisor is meant to give guidance from at least the same level, and the pairing follows the advisor tool's compatibility table.
check: After changing the agent model, check the advisor compatibility table and change the advisor if the new pairing would be rejected.
quote: the agent’s own model must not be more capable than its advisor; models of equal capability can pair.

claim: Managed Agents advisor consultations are billed at the advisor model's rates and count toward the session budget, and each consultation sends the advisor the primary thread's conversation so far, so consultations late in a long session cost more input tokens.
why: The advisor reads the whole primary conversation each time, with caching handled automatically.
check: Check whether an advisor is consulted at moments that justify its input and cost, especially in a long session where each consultation sends the conversation so far.
quote: Each consultation sends the advisor the primary thread’s conversation so far, so consultations late in a long session use more input tokens.

claim: Updating a Managed Agents agent from the coordinator type to multiagent_20261001 replaces the whole multiagent block, so an update that omits the subagent list or advisor leaves the list empty and the advisor disabled; once on the new type, omitted settings keep their stored value.
why: The first update replaces rather than merges, and the new type also turns on workflows and inline agents by default.
check: For a migration to multiagent_20261001, check that the update resends any subagents and advisor that should be kept and that sessions using the new block are created after the update.
quote: The update replaces the whole `multiagent` block, so send the list of agents and the advisor again, as the example does.

claim: Managed Agents subagent threads accept follow-up messages and keep prior turns until archived, while the agent cannot send follow-ups to a workflow run's threads and the server archives them by the end of the run.
why: Subagents are driven by the agent, while a workflow is a program that passes context and results programmatically.
check: Use subagent threads if the primary agent needs to send a follow-up to the same worker and have it retain its prior turns.
quote: The agent can’t send follow-up messages to a run’s threads, and the server archives each one by the end of its run.

claim: In Managed Agents an outcome pairs a description with a required Markdown rubric, and the harness provisions a grader with a separate context window to avoid influence from the main agent's implementation choices.
why: The grader reports which criteria passed or failed, and the harness gives that feedback to the agent for the next iteration.
check: For an agent loop that decides 'done' by asking the same agent whether it is finished, compare with this separate-grader design.
quote: The grader uses a separate context window to avoid being influenced by the main agent’s implementation choices.

claim: Anthropic recommends explicit criteria that a Managed Agents outcome grader can score independently.
why: Vague criteria make independent per-criterion evaluations noisy.
check: Check for criteria that name a verifiable condition, such as a CSV price column containing numeric values.
quote: The grader scores each criterion independently, so vague criteria produce noisy evaluations.

claim: When creating a Claude Managed Agents outcome rubric from scratch, Anthropic suggests giving Claude a known-good artifact to analyze and turning its analysis into the rubric, which often works better than writing criteria with no example.
why: Starting from a concrete good example grounds the criteria in what quality looks like for this task.
check: If a Claude Managed Agents outcome needs a rubric and none exists, check whether a known-good artifact is available to derive the criteria from.
quote: try giving Claude an example of a known-good artifact and asking it to analyze what makes that content good, then turn that analysis into a rubric.

claim: A Managed Agents outcome's max_iterations defaults to 3 with a maximum of 20, and a max_iterations_reached result triggers one final acknowledgment turn before the session goes idle without further evaluation.
why: The iteration cap bounds the grade-and-revise loop; the result values are satisfied, needs_revision, max_iterations_reached, failed and interrupted.
check: Check that the effective max_iterations fits the task and that callers distinguish max_iterations_reached from satisfied.
quote: # "max_iterations" is optional; default 3, max 20

claim: A Managed Agents outcome evaluation returns failed when the rubric does not apply to the deliverables.
why: A failed evaluation sends the session to idle and ends the revision cycle.
check: Check whether the outcome description and rubric contradict each other or the rubric otherwise fails to apply to the requested deliverables.
quote: Returned when the rubric does not apply to the deliverables, for example if the description and rubric contradict each other.

claim: A Managed Agents memory store is a workspace-scoped collection of text documents exposed to the agent through its standard file tools under /mnt/memory/ as a live mount in a hosted sandbox or a worker-synced copy in a supported self-hosted sandbox, with the location described in the system prompt.
why: The agent toolset is required to read and write the store, which lets the agent carry information across sessions that start with fresh context by default.
check: Check that agents that should learn across sessions have the agent toolset enabled and a store attached, and that the store's description tells the agent what is in it.
quote: The agent reads and writes it with the same file tools it uses for the rest of the filesystem, and a note describing each mount is automatically added to the system prompt, telling the agent where to look.

claim: Managed Agents memory stores attach with read_write access by default, and a successful prompt injection in an agent that handles untrusted input could write malicious content that later sessions read as trusted memory, so reference material and shared lookups should be attached read_only.
why: Memory persists across sessions, so a poisoned note outlives the session that wrote it.
check: For agents that read web pages, user uploads or third-party tool output, check that stores are read_only unless the agent must write.
quote: a successful prompt injection could write malicious content into the store. Later sessions then read that content as trusted memory.

claim: A Managed Agents session can attach at most 8 memory stores, a store holds at most 10,000 memories, and once the store is full writes to new memories fail while existing ones stay readable and editable.
why: Anthropic suggests focused stores and pruning before the limit, with a fresh writable store and a read-only original when the original has grown beyond its useful scope.
check: Check agents that append one note per event for unbounded memory growth and for a pruning or consolidation plan.
quote: When a store reaches its 10,000-memory limit, writes to new memories fail

claim: Managed Agents memory stores can be attached only when a session is created; adding or removing one in a running session is not supported.
why: Unlike file resources, the mount is fixed at creation.
check: Check that session creation attaches every required memory store and that any optional store-specific instructions are supplied there within the 4,096-character cap.
quote: Unlike file resources, memory stores can only be attached at session creation time; adding or removing one from a running session is not supported.

claim: On Managed Agents memory store calls with explicit beta headers, use agent-memory-2026-07-22 in place of managed-agents-2026-04-01 because sending both returns 400, though listing a store's memories works under either header alone and session endpoints still use managed-agents-2026-04-01.
why: The two betas are mutually exclusive on memory store requests.
check: Check that requests with explicit headers never combine the two betas on a memory store call and that session endpoints use managed-agents-2026-04-01.
quote: Don’t combine `agent-memory-2026-07-22` with `managed-agents-2026-04-01` on a memory store request: sending both returns a `400` error.

claim: Managed Agents memory versions are retained for 30 days after they are written, though recent versions of a live memory are always kept, and there is no restore endpoint, so rollback means reading an old version and writing its content back.
why: The versions record who changed what, and exporting them preserves a copy of the audit history beyond the service's retention window.
check: If memory edits must be auditable beyond 30 days, check that versions are exported through the API.
quote: Versions are retained for 30 days after they are written; however, the recent versions of a live memory are always kept regardless of age

claim: Anthropic recommends smaller purpose-built Managed Agents memory stores over one catch-all store and offers a dreaming session as an option for consolidating fragmented content into a separate output store.
why: Each store has its own 10,000-memory limit and scoped write access makes growth traceable.
check: Look for catch-all stores that could be split, read-only consumers with write access, and dreaming configurations that assume consolidation rewrites the original store.
quote: Rather than one large general-purpose store, use smaller purpose-built stores: one for each user, one for shared domain knowledge, and one for project-specific context.

claim: Within the Managed Agents beta, MCP tunnels and dreaming are in a more limited research preview that needs a separate access request.
why: They are not enabled by default for API accounts, unlike the rest of Managed Agents.
check: A setup that depends on dreaming or MCP tunnels needs confirmation that research-preview access was granted.
quote: [MCP tunnels](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/overview) and [dreaming](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/dreams) are in a more limited research preview. To enable them, [request access to the research preview](https://claude.com/form/claude-managed-agents).

claim: On Anthropic's CL-Bench memory task, telling Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 simply that a memory folder exists was enough, while a fixed rule such as 'record only failures' cost them much of the gain from memory.
why: For stronger models, freedom to judge what is salient worked better than rules set in advance, and fixed rules could weaken performance.
check: If a task on Opus 5 or Opus 4.7 uses a fixed rule such as recording only failures, compare its results with simple guidance that a memory folder is available.
quote: When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right).

claim: For frontier Claude models Anthropic typically gives simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks or when something is clearly worth remembering, and leaves the rest of the judgment to Claude.
why: In the CL-Bench database task, simply telling Claude that a memory folder was available was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use it effectively.
check: For a frontier Claude setup, check whether prescribed memory formats or triggers serve a purpose beyond the simple guidance Anthropic typically uses.
quote: With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.

claim: On Anthropic's CL-Bench database task, Sonnet 4.6 often skipped reading memory and failed to test its theories unprompted, but instructions to read memory before answering and test theories nearly doubled its score, while Sonnet 5 read memory before answering 9 out of 10 times without prompting.
why: In this task, Sonnet 4.6 read memory less than half the time without prompting, while Sonnet 5 usually did so on its own.
check: If a similar task depends on consulting memory before answering or testing theories, evaluate whether explicit guidance helps on the Sonnet model in use.
quote: In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.

claim: In Anthropic's Pokémon Red runs, Fable 5 wrote nine memory files plus a global.md dashboard for goals, plans, and rules, Opus 5.5 kept a small folder tracking its goal and next steps, and Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 files and spent more time tending stale records.
why: In the game, changing information visible on every turn was redundant to store, while strategies, plans, and tested rules needed to be written down to persist.
check: Check whether an agent stores changing state it can already read from its environment and whether it preserves plans and tested rules it cannot recover that way.
quote:
Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).
Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md

claim: Anthropic advises keeping preloaded memory small and moving details to linked notes because injected memories consume tokens, can carry an incorrect note into every session, and do not guarantee Claude will act on them.
why: Longer instruction files reduce adherence, and Claude Code's auto memory keeps its injected layer small the same way by loading only the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md as an index.
check: Check a global instruction file or MEMORY.md for length and for detailed notes that should be moved to linked files.
quote: Injected memories use up valuable tokens, and an incorrect note can be carried into every session. Loading a note also doesn’t guarantee that Claude acts on it: our documentation on Claude Code warns that longer instruction files reduce adherence.

claim: Claude can read and trust an incorrect or stale memory note in a later session, and Anthropic describes dreaming as one way to check notes against original transcripts and correct mistakes.
why: In Anthropic's Pokémon run with an incorrect landmark note, Claude dropped back to the earlier route three times, while dreaming checked the note against the transcript and corrected it.
check: Check whether persistent notes likely to be wrong or to drift can be checked against the original evidence and corrected.
quote: a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.

claim: In Anthropic's LAB contract task, 41 of 57 graded facts survived when several agents wrote to one shared wiki table, while 57 of 57 survived when one agent per contract quoted the terms verbatim on its own page.
why: In the shared table, the agents overwrote one another's work and the summaries captured some contract terms poorly or omitted them altogether.
check: For a multi-agent wiki that must preserve exact terms, check whether agents have separate pages to avoid overwrites and quote the terms they need to preserve.
quote: How many graded contract facts made it into the wiki, before and after instructions changed. Left: several agents writing to one shared page; 41 of 57 facts survived. Right: one agent per contract, each writing its own page and quoting terms word for word; 57 of 57 facts survived.

claim: In Anthropic's Stainless test on about 350,000 files, search with an Opus 5-built wiki scored 54% to 61% as the wiki grew, compared with 53% for search alone.
why: The wiki alone topped out at 48% in the same test, so it was most useful alongside search.
check: Before recommending an agent-maintained wiki, compare search with and without it on the target questions.
quote: When it used both search and the wiki, Claude’s aggregate score rose from 54% to 61% as that wiki grew, compared with 53% when it had access to the search tool alone.

claim: Anthropic's orchestration-mode example combines a documented effort level, a mid-conversation system message that announces the mode, and standing consent in the orchestration tool's description.
why: The mode uses documented API building blocks and preserves the cached prefix by keeping the top-level system field fixed.
check: Check that the implementation uses the documented effort range and that its model and platform support mid-conversation system messages.
quote:
The mode is not an API parameter. It is built entirely from documented pieces:

1. **An effort level:** requests run at a documented [Effort](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort) value such as `xhigh`. There is no hidden level above the ones on that page.

claim: Anthropic's example leaves the top-level system prompt unchanged and adds a role system message after a user turn for mode entry, a one-line refresher every 10 user turns while active, or mode exit, preserving the cached prefix ahead of the message.
why: Appending the system message after the user turn satisfies the placement rule and leaves preceding cached content unchanged.
check: If a harness switches modes by changing the top-level system prompt mid-session, it invalidates the cache on each switch; check whether a mid-conversation message would do.
quote: Placing the system message after the user turn keeps every cached byte ahead of it untouched, and satisfies the placement rule that a system message follows a user turn.

claim: Anthropic's pattern for conditional behavior keeps the mode reminders short and puts the heavyweight instructions (opt-in rule, standing consent, granularity guidance, quality patterns) in the tool description, which the reminders point to.
why: The reminders can stay short and occasional because the tool description contains the detailed instructions for using the tool.
check: Look for long mode or policy text repeated in the system prompt or per-turn messages that could live in the tool description with a short pointer.
quote: The reminders are short on purpose. They flip the mode and point at the tool description, where the heavyweight instructions live. The full text is sent once when the mode turns on, the refresher is re-sent only after several user turns, and the exit notice is sent once when the mode turns off.

claim: In Anthropic's orchestration-mode example each fan-out subagent runs at the same effort as the main loop, and a single request can spawn many subagent conversations, so the mode multiplies token use and should be reserved for work that justifies the cost.
why: The example passes the same xhigh effort setting explicitly to the main loop and each subagent request.
check: When adapting the fan-out example, check the worker effort setting and whether the work that triggers fan-out justifies its token cost.
quote: The fan-out itself multiplies token usage: a single request can spawn many subagent conversations, so reserve the mode for work that justifies the cost.

claim: Anthropic's example runs a second wave of agents that re-derive findings from sources and default to refuted when uncertain, and its tool description suggests an inline scout before fan-out and a completeness critic to look for omissions.
why: Re-deriving findings from sources gives the orchestrator a second assessment to weigh alongside the original result.
check: For multi-agent reviews or audits, check whether findings are verified by independent agents against the source and not accepted on the worker's own report.
quote: every verifier re-derives the claims from the source, defaulting to refuted when uncertain.

claim: Anthropic's example scopes each fan-out subtask to a distinct concern, component, or question and says a focused review of a module of a few hundred lines rarely needs more than about ten subtasks.
why: The tool description scales fan-out to the work requested, allowing more subtasks for a broad audit than for a focused review.
check: Check that subtasks address distinct concerns without splitting by line or file section, and that the fan-out size fits the requested scope.
quote:
Scale the count to what the user asked for: a "
          "focused review of a module of a few hundred lines rarely needs more than about ten "
          "subtasks; a broad audit of a large codebase can justify more.

claim: Anthropic's example resumes fan-out by reusing journaled results keyed by the SHA-256 of their exact prompts, and the production guidance suggests a hard cap on total subagents launched across the session.
why: Restarting dozens of subagents from scratch is expensive, and a per-call cap does not bound a runaway plan across calls.
check: For an expensive fan-out harness that must resume after interruption, check that it can recover journaled results for the same prompts and caps launches across the whole session.
quote: A small content-addressed journal makes it idempotent: before dispatching a subagent, look up the SHA-256 of its prompt in a local JSON file, and return the recorded result if one exists.

claim: Managed Agents keeps the full event log outside Claude's context window in a durable session that the harness can read by position with getEvents().
why: Positional reads let the harness resume reading or revisit events around a specific action.
check: If earlier events matter to a Managed Agents harness, check that it requests the needed event range from the session log.
quote: But rather than be stored within the sandbox or REPL, context is durably stored in the session log. The interface, getEvents(), allows the brain to interrogate context by selecting positional slices of the event stream.

claim: Anthropic recommends Managed Agents subagents when the main agent needs to follow up after a report or needs specialists you list with their own prompts and tools.
why: A subagent's session thread accepts follow-ups until it is archived.
check: Check that work needing follow-ups stays on a subagent thread and that specialist subagents are listed with the prompts and tools they need.
quote: The agent should follow up with a subagent after it reports, or it needs specialists that you list, with their own system prompts and tools.

claim: Anthropic recommends a Managed Agents advisor when a single agent should do the work and seek a second model's judgment at key moments.
why: The main agent can consult the advisor mid-turn and continue doing the work itself.
check: Check whether work done by a single agent calls for an advisor at planning or final review.
quote: One agent should do the work, with an advisor model’s judgment at key moments such as planning or a final review.

claim: A Managed Agents session supports one active outcome at a time.
why: The session can start a new outcome after the previous one finishes and retains its history.
check: Check that callers wait for the prior outcome's terminal span.outcome_evaluation_end event before sending another user.define_outcome event.
quote: Only one outcome is supported at a time, but you can chain outcomes in sequence. To do this, send a new `user.define_outcome` event after the terminal `span.outcome_evaluation_end` event of the previous outcome.

claim: In Anthropic's Stainless test, using search with the Opus 5-built wiki saved about 20,000 tokens per question.
why: Wiki maintenance takes compute, so query savings and total costs can differ.
check: When testing whether a wiki saves tokens on the target questions, measure query usage and account for the compute needed to keep the wiki accurate.
quote: Using search and the wiki also saved about 20,000 tokens per question.

claim: In a Harvey LAB task where most rubric criteria could be met from a single document, Anthropic found no clear performance gain from a wiki over search alone.
why: A text search within one document often surfaced the evidence needed for the brief.
check: Before adding a wiki for similar work, check how often direct search in one document supplies the needed evidence.
quote:
Most criteria could be met from a single document.
In other cases, the wiki was less useful. On one LAB task (Figure 11, right), brief criteria often could be retrieved with a text search from a single document, and the wiki showed no clear gain in performance relative to search.

claim: On a Harvey LAB task in Anthropic's study, the agent-built wiki grew larger than the source documents.
why: The wiki retained so much detail that it provided little abstraction.
check: When a wiki is meant to condense a corpus, check whether it takes up more space than the source documents.
quote: On another LAB task, the wiki grew larger than the documents themselves (Figure 12).
